case_study_insert.main_stem: VerdeMix Concrete (VMC) is a public limited company in the green concrete sector, employing a workforce of 110. Founded in 2014 by Maria Doyle, the business produces low-carbon precast blocks made with GGBS and recycled aggregates for infrastructure and housing projects, and operates a flat organisational structure with autocratic leadership. VMC plans to invest $1,750,000 in acquiring a recycled aggregate washing and batching facility, financed by a $1,000,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $1,350,000 a year, a variable cost of $45.00 a unit and a selling price of $75.00, and currently produces 104,000 units a year. VMC faces two operational problems: two lost-time injuries in 2026 and absenteeism has reached 9%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — October 2026: The batching plant produced 19,500 units last quarter; the defect rate fell to 1.6% from 2.7% a year ago. Two lost-time injuries were recorded this year and absenteeism stands at 9%. Average order-to-delivery time is 2.1 days against a 1.5-day target. 34 of 110 staff have not completed silica-dust refresher training; the course costs $700 per employee. A new rail-depot contract is worth $2.1 million over two years.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of VerdeMix Concrete for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.5% to 6.25% in October 2026. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.8% from $12.50 to $13.35 per hour from April 2027, raising plant and batching payroll costs. (3) GGBS, cement and aggregate input costs have risen 13.6% year-on-year, while infrastructure spending on rail and housing grew 5.4% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VMC plans to finance the recycled aggregate facility with a $1,000,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for VMC of using retained profit rather than enlarging the share issue further.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit funds the $750,000 portion with no new shares, so existing shareholders' ownership, dividend rights and control are diluted as little as possible; every extra diluted share cedes both earnings and voting influence that Maria Doyle and the founding team worked to keep when VMC went public. It also avoids underwriting fees and the placing discount typically demanded by institutional buyers, stretching the $1,000,000 issue further and keeping the acquisition fully funded.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no interest, dividend or repayment obligation of any kind, unlike the $1,000,000 share issue alternative of deeper equity or any loan, so VMC keeps flexibility to fund the recycled aggregate washing facility's silica-dust safety upgrades for 34 uncertified staff or additional batching capacity if the $2.1 million rail-depot contract extends. It also signals genuine cash generation to the market, supporting the share price that enabled the issue and reassuring infrastructure clients of VMC's financial stability.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to VerdeMix Concrete and its acquisition decision.

questions.question_text: VMC is launching its low-carbon GGBS block range for infrastructure contractors. Consider a stand at a national infrastructure expo, advertising in trade magazines, or a LinkedIn B2B campaign. Which should VMC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National infrastructure expo: A stand at the major annual expo would put VMC directly in front of rail and housing contractors, allow full-size blocks to be inspected and crushed/cracked in live demonstrations, and generate same-week leads — powerful for the $2.1 million rail-depot contract and GGBS specification discussions. Drawbacks: stand fees and three days of senior staff time are expensive, reach is one-off, and competitor aggregates and Portland-cement incumbents exhibit alongside VMC for attention.

Trade-magazine advertising: Civil engineering and concrete trade journals reach the exact specification engineers and procurement officers who write GGBS block schedules into tender documents; adverts can feature the 1.6% defect rate, 5.4% infrastructure growth and the $75.00 delivered price, and can be timed to budget-setting cycles. Passive and print-based, it informs but cannot show block performance hands-on, and readership overlaps among titles.

LinkedIn B2B campaign: Targeted posts and sponsored content aimed at infrastructure roles (rail, housing, highways) can carry case studies, carbon calculations and the 13.6% input-cost savings story, cheaply and measurably. Reach builds slowly, engagement varies, and it cannot replace the trust of face-to-face technical sign-off that infrastructure buyers demand for structural products.

Recommendation: VMC should choose trade-magazine advertising. It delivers continuous, targeted coverage across the whole infrastructure buying cycle at low cost per specification decision, and it directly counters the Portland-cement incumbents writing against VMC's blocks. The expo is rejected as a valuable one-off complement but not a launch backbone; LinkedIn is rejected as too slow and indirect for a high-stakes structural specification decision, though it should run alongside at low cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VMC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VMC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the expo and LinkedIn are rejected as primary channels.

questions.question_text: VMC's absenteeism has reached 9% and two lost-time injuries occurred in 2026. Explain two benefits for VMC of its flat organisational structure.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure with very few management layers lets Maria Doyle and the plant manager speak directly with batching, washing and forklift crews about silica-dust controls, guarding isolation and the 1.5-day delivery target — safety instructions travel fast instead of through a chain of command, directly attacking the two lost-time injuries and supporting refresher training for 34 of 110 staff before the recycled aggregate washing plant opens and adds new machinery hazards.

Point 2: The short chain of command also means absenteeism hotspots are spotted within hours and cover or welfare support is arranged same-shift without paperwork, and workers feel closer to leadership so their concerns about hazards, rotas and pay are heard quickly rather than escalated formally through layers of supervision. This lifts morale, supports attendance, and protects the 104,000-unit annual output behind the $2.1 million rail-depot contract and the quality turnaround (defects down to 1.6% from 2.7%).

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VMC's safety record, absenteeism and delivery pipeline.

questions.question_text: VMC must certify 34 staff in silica-dust safety and forklift operation before the new facility starts. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at an external safety academy. Which should VMC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Off-the-job training: An accredited safety academy would give all 34 staff certificated teaching on silica-dust control, respirator fit and forklift licensing, producing audit-ready documentation for inspectors and rail-depot clients. Cost is roughly $23,800 (34 × $700), affordable within the $1,750,000 facility budget. Academy peers share cross-company practice, trainers are undistracted by production, and the certificates carry weight with clients. Drawbacks: two to three days away from the line per worker, generic content not tuned to VMC's batch geometry, and respirator fit still needs machine-side verification to be safe.

On-the-job training: Coaching by experienced VMC crew at the batching plant is machine-specific, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 104,000-unit output and the 2.1-day delivery promise intact while workers learn the exact silica and forklift hazards in their own bay with real machinery and dust readings. However, trainers may pass on shortcuts, records may not satisfy external clients or inspectors, and learning beside active batches carries the precise near-miss risk VMC is eliminating after two lost-time injuries and 9% absenteeism.

Decision: VMC should choose on-the-job training for the silica and forklift modules, supplemented by one short off-the-job awareness day for compliance and certification anchoring. The machine-side context is where silica exposure and forklift movements actually occur, output and rail-depot deadlines cannot pause, and the flat structure lets Maria Doyle monitor competency personally; $23,800 in fees would also divert cash from the $750,000 retained-profit leg of the acquisition. Pure off-the-job training is rejected because generic classroom content cannot certify competence on VMC's actual machines and would stop the line against a live order book.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VMC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of VMC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of VMC with a well-justified decision covering cost, legal compliance and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VMC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,350,000 ÷ ($75.00 − $45.00) = $1,350,000 ÷ $30.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $75.00 − $45.00 = $30.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $30.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VMC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. VMC's managers can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 104,000 units to confirm the batching expansion is comfortably above the profit threshold, with a margin of safety of 59,000 units, informing whether to commit to the recycled aggregates washing plant.
2. Contribution per unit of $30.00 lets VMC model tender pricing: for example, matching an incumbent's $68.00 price cuts contribution to $23.00, and managers can check the reduced margin still covers the $1,350,000 fixed costs before locking bid prices for the $2.1 million rail-depot work.
3. The unit cost of $57.98 a unit ($6,030,000 total costs ÷ 104,000 units) can be benchmarked quarter by quarter to expose defects and idle batching time, target the 1.6% defect rate still lower and set purchase prices for GGBS against the 13.6% input-cost inflation.
4. Knowing break-even output helps managers set production targets for the batching schedule, check the $1,000,000 share issue plus $750,000 retained profit funds the facility without overstretch, and decide bonus thresholds for hitting 104,000 units safely after two lost-time injuries.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $30.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 59,000 units; tender modelling at $30.00 contribution against rail-depot pricing; unit cost benchmarking at $57.98 against input inflation; and expansion feasibility checks on the $1,750,000 facility.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VMC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VMC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 33.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 38.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $6,900,000 revenue − $4,623,000 cost of sales = $2,277,000; 2025 gross profit = $7,800,000 revenue − $4,836,000 cost of sales = $2,964,000. Operating profit rose from $1,035,000 to $1,404,000. Capital employed rose from $5,750,000 to $6,240,000. 2024: $2,277,000 ÷ $6,900,000 = 33.0%; $1,035,000 ÷ $6,900,000 = 15.0%; $1,035,000 ÷ $5,750,000 = 18.0%. 2025: $2,964,000 ÷ $7,800,000 = 38.0%; $1,404,000 ÷ $7,800,000 = 18.0%; $1,404,000 ÷ $6,240,000 = 22.5%.

Evaluation: Performance has improved convincingly. Revenue grew 13.0% to $7,800,000 and gross profit jumped by $687,000 — driven by the GGBS mix premium, defect reduction to 1.6% and rail-depot volumes — while cost of sales grew only 4.6%, so manufacturing discipline is compounding. Operating profit rose 35.7% even after interest payable climbed from $240,000 to $285,000, meaning the improvement came from operations, not financial engineering. Capital employed grew 8.5% to $6,240,000, comfortably outpaced by profit growth; 2026 requires absorbing the $1,750,000 recycled-aggregates facility, which will dilute returns temporarily while washing plant commissioning completes, and the 13.6% input-cost inflation will test margin discipline.

Conclusion: VMC's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit, operating profit and every return measure (33.0% to 38.0%, 15.0% to 18.0%, 18.0% to 22.5%) moved decisively upward against capital employed growing more slowly. The business should lock in gains by commissioning the facility on budget, renegotiating GGBS supply and fixing the rate risk on future borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether VMC's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VMC of vertical integration into recycled aggregate washing and batching.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Vertical integration gives VMC control of its aggregate feedstock, shielding the $45.00 variable cost per unit from the 13.6% year-on-year input-cost inflation in Appendix 3, cutting GGBS-equivalent exposure and removing a supplier margin VMC currently pays on every one of the 104,000 units produced. It also secures supply for the $2.1 million rail-depot contract, supports marketing the blocks as fully recycled-content, and captures the profit of washing and batching inside VMC rather than in an upstream supplier.

Disadvantage: The $1,750,000 facility demands heavy capital at the same time as VMC is already carrying $285,000 interest payable and must fund 34 staff silica-dust recertification; integration risk is real — a loss-maker inherits legacy liabilities, and management attention shifts from VMC's batching core at a time when announcements in the injury log and 9% absenteeism still need resolving. If infrastructure spending (currently +5.4%) flattens, the added fixed costs of the washing plant could compress the recently earned $30.00 contribution per unit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VMC's vertical integration, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 6.8% minimum wage increase and the 13.6% rise in input costs will affect VMC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): VMC is an ex-dividend public limited company funded mainly by equity (the $1,000,000 share issue) and retained profit ($750,000), so direct interest exposure is limited — roughly $285,000 interest payable in 2025, a 0.75-point rise adding little on current borrowing. The bigger effect is demand: at 6.25% mortgage and development-finance costs squeeze housing approvals (+5.4% recently), delaying order decisions and pressure-testing the $2.1 million rail-depot timetable. Manageable, but strategically not ignorable.

Minimum wage rise (6.8%, to $13.35 per hour from April 2027): With 110 mainly plant and batching staff on hourly pay, the award adds about $0.85 per hour; at around 2,000 hours a year per employee, that is roughly $1,700 per worker or about $187,000 a year — around 13% of operating profit. The two lost-time injuries and 9% absenteeism already inflate overtime coverage; the certified forklift and silica roles will command above-minimum rates anyway. Mechanisation of the new wash plant will offset part of this.

Input-cost inflation (13.6% GGBS, cement and aggregate): VMC's $45.00 variable cost is dominated by binders and aggregates. If materials are 60% of variable cost (about $27.00), a 13.6% rise adds roughly $3.67 per unit; across 104,000 units that is about $382,000 a year — two to three times the wage award and many times the interest effect, directly eroding the $30.00 contribution per unit unless passed through in tender repricing.

Conclusion: The 13.6% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It scales with every one of the 104,000 units produced, outweighs the wage and interest effects several times over, and challenges the $75.00 price point directly before the recycled-aggregates plant delivers input savings. The wage increase is second (large but mechanisable); the interest-rate rise is smallest in cash but the greatest demand risk. VMC must lock GGBS supply contracts, renegotiate depot tenders with energy/material surcharges, and commission the wash plant on schedule to claw back input dependence.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to VMC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VMC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VMC with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
